about: TOWN GAMES AND PASTIMES, 793 to 1066: what people of the North Sea world really played, and how each plays in the game as a small board or a run of cards. Ten games: for the acts dice, tafl, song, riddles and drink, and for the contests that come as cards. Every game has its evidence, what is not known, complete rules, stakes and what it gives. A draft in the game's own files, for the user to overwrite. Written 4 Oct 2026 by the town-games writer; the page that goes with it is Design/town_games.md. A fact that could not be checked carries (?).
rules_for_all: The clock stands still while a game is open. When it closes, the game has cost the time in 'takes' and counts as one talk of the call.
Odds are said as a word, never a number: sure, likely, doubtful (the words of knowing_793.json).
No game can take the boat, the debt or the player's freedom. A silver stake is never more than a tenth of the silver aboard, and the other man must have the stake to lay it.
Every game can be left at the cost of pride only, and no game only punishes: the loser still has the talk (a rumour, a riddle, a man who knows him now).
A man plays one game with you in an evening and remembers who won. The same man will not play the same game again for three days.
Riddles, song and matching men need the other man's tongue (tongue 0.5 or more, or a crewman who has it). Dice, the boards, wrestling and horses need no tongue at all, which is why sailors play them.
The rules are the same for the other man as for the player. He plays by his temper (bold, careful, proud), which the card says in plain words before the stake is laid.

games.name: The high throw
games.screen: cards, with two dice drawn on the card
evidence: Salme on Saaremaa, about 700 to 750: two ships with 41 men from central Sweden, killed abroad and buried with hundreds of gaming pieces of whalebone and antler and six dice.
Birka, chamber grave Bj 581, about 940 to 950: three dice and 28 gaming pieces (one of them a king) in a bag in the lap of the dead, and the iron frame of a board beside the body.

Konungahella, about 1020 (?): Olaf of Norway and Olof of the Svear cast dice for a district on Hising, 'he who threw the highest should have the district'. The Swede threw two sixes twice. Olaf threw two sixes, then a six and a die that split and showed seven eyes. (Snorri, written about 1230.)
Tacitus on the Germans, about AD 98, seven hundred years before the game begins: 'on the last and final throw they stake the freedom of their own persons'.
Wulfstan of York's rules for priests, about 1005: a priest is not to be a hunter, a hawker or a 'taeflere' (a player at the tables), but to play on his books (?). So priests did.

Dice of the North are bone or antler, and many are long rather than square, so the one and the two at the ends seldom come up (?). Sheep's ankle bones (knucklebones) are the poor man's dice everywhere since Rome; a fifth-century urn at Caistor-by-Norwich held some thirty of them with gaming pieces, one cut with runes (?).
games.not_known: No rule of any dice game was written down in these years. All the sources give is the kings' rule at Konungahella: two dice, the highest throw wins, equal throws are thrown again. The choice to stand or throw again is the game's own, kept as small as it can be. The worth of a knucklebone's four sides (1, 3, 4, 6) is Roman; what the North counted is not known.
games.where: Any quay, beach market or ale-house, and aboard at anchor. In halls among the household men. Not in a minster, and not before a priest who keeps his rule.
how_it_plays: Two play. Each lays the same stake on the hatch or the bench. The least is 1 d; the most is what the poorer of the two has by him.
The man who was challenged throws first. A throw is two dice, and the eyes are added: 2 to 12.
He may stand on his throw, or take the dice up and throw once more. The second throw stands, whatever it is.
Then the other man does the same, seeing what he has to beat.
The higher throw takes both stakes. Equal throws are thrown again, as the kings did.
The winner of a round throws first in the next, so the loser sees what he must beat.
After a round the loser may ask for another at the same stake or at double. The winner may say no and keep what he has. Three rounds are an evening, and nobody thinks less of a man who stops there.

Knucklebones, where nobody owns dice: four sheep's ankle bones are thrown together. Each lies on one of four sides, worth 1, 3, 4 and 6. Four different sides up beats everything; otherwise the higher sum wins. Turns and the second throw are as above. The stake is a cup of ale or a penny.

False dice: when he has won twice running you may ask to throw with his dice. If they are false you take back all you lost to him this evening and the room knows him. If they are true he is cold with you for a season.
games.card_run: Card 1: who he is, his temper, the stake he offers (take it, name a smaller one, or leave). Card 2: his throw and whether he stood; your throw; stand or throw again, with the odds of beating him as a word. Card 3: who took it; another round, double, look at his dice, or stop.
games.odds_words: To beat a throw of 4 or less: sure. Of 5 or 6: likely. Of 7 or 8: doubtful. Of 9 or more the card says it plainly: 'only a ten or better will do.'
games.stakes: 1 to 12 d a round on a quay; up to 60 d in a hall. A man with no silver left may stake a thing (a knife, a comb, a cloak pin). A man with nothing left at all may stake himself, as Tacitus tells of an older time: in the game that is a season at your oars without pay. The player can never stake his boat, his debt or himself.
games.what_it_gives: Silver, won or lost a little at a time. A rumour: a man who has thrown three rounds with you talks, and what he tells is as old as the ship he came on. A friend if you lose well or stop when he asks; a cold face if you take his last penny. Standing in the harbour if you show up a cheat. Once in a long while, a hand for a season.
games.picture: Two men kneeling at an upturned tub on a quay at dusk, two bone dice between them, a small heap of cut silver and pennies, a third man watching with a cup.
games.source: Heimskringla, Saga of Olaf Haraldson ch. 97 (Laing 1844: gutenberg.org/ebooks/598); Tacitus, Germania 24 (Church and Brodribb 1877: sourcebooks.fordham.edu/source/tacitus1.html); Salme: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salme_ships; Birka Bj 581: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birka_female_Viking_warrior; knucklebone values: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knucklebones; the Canons of Edgar (?), the Caistor-by-Norwich urn (?) and the shape of northern dice (?) are from memory, not checked.

games.name: Tafl (the king's table)
games.screen: a board on screen: 9 by 9 squares, 25 pieces (the small 7 by 7 pegged board in Gaelic ports)
evidence: Gokstad ship burial, Vestfold, ship built about 890 and buried about 900 to 905 (?): a piece of a wooden board with 13 by 13 squares on one side and nine men's morris on the other, and a playing piece of horn.
Ballinderry, Co. Westmeath, found 1932: a wooden board of the 900s with 7 by 7 peg holes, the middle and the corners marked (?), thought to be Dublin or Manx work (?).
Birka: many glass playing pieces; and grave Bj 581 (about 940 to 950) had 28 pieces with a king, three dice and an iron-bound board.
Salme, about 700 to 750: hundreds of whalebone and antler pieces with the dead of two ships; one man is said to have had a king piece in his mouth (?).

York, Coppergate, 900s: a piece of an oak board with a row of 15 squares (?). Toftanes in the Faroes, 900s: a board with tafl on one side and morris on the other (?). Hedeby: pieces of bone, amber and glass, dice and board fragments (?). Lindisfarne: a small worked piece of blue glass of the 700s or 800s. Trondheim: an 11 by 11 board, but of the 1100s.

Alea evangelii, 'the game of the gospel': a drawing of an 18 by 18 board and its men in an Irish hand (Oxford, Corpus Christi College MS 122), said to have been made at King Athelstan's court (924 to 939) and taken to Ireland by Dub Innse, bishop of Bangor (died 953). It is tafl dressed as a harmony of the gospels, with no rules.

Words: the Exeter Book's maxims (copied about 970) have two men sit at the board while their troubles slip from them (?). The young lords of Rigsthula learn 'sund ok tafl', swimming and tafl (?). Gestumblindi's riddle: 'Who are the maids that fight weaponless around their lord; the brown ever sheltering, the fair ever attacking him?' (riddle r-gest-19 in the chest; also r-gest-25 and r-gest-31).

Roskilde, the day before Michaelmas 1026 (?): King Canute took back a false move against Earl Ulf; the earl threw over the board and walked out, and was killed in church the next morning. Snorri, two hundred years on, calls the game chess.
games.not_known: Nobody in these years wrote the rules down. Boards, pieces and riddles survive. The only rules written by a man who watched the game are Linnaeus's notes on tablut among the Sami in 1732, nine hundred years late: a 9 by 9 board, eight 'Swedes' and their king against sixteen 'Muscovites'. His Latin was put into English in 1811 with a mistake (a king taken only when shut in on four sides), and most modern rule sets carry it. The rules here follow Linnaeus as he is now read. Who moves first, whether the king may take, how the empty seat counts, and whether the king must reach an edge or a corner on the bigger boards are guesses. The board's help line says so.
games.where: Norse halls, ale-houses and ships at anchor; Dublin from 841; York under the Danes from 866; English halls, where it is 'taefl'. At Dorestad and the Frisian quays only when Danes or Northmen lie there. Not played by Franks (their board game is tables, with dice: see 'left_out').
how_it_plays: The board is 9 squares by 9. The middle square is the king's seat. The king stands on it with eight men of his own: two out along each of the four arms of a cross. These are the dark men. Sixteen fair men stand against them, four at the middle of each side: three along the edge and one in front of the middle one.
The fair side, the attackers, moves first. After that the sides move in turn, one piece a turn.
Every piece, the king too, moves in a straight line along a row or a column, as far as the squares are empty. No piece jumps another and none moves slantwise.
Only the king may stand on the king's seat. No other piece may stop on it or pass over it.

Taking: when your move puts an enemy man between two of yours, in line along a row or a column, he is taken off the board. It must be your move that closes the trap: a man may step between two enemies and stand there safe. One move can take two or three men at once. The king may be one of the two that take.
The empty seat counts as an enemy to both sides: a man standing next to it is taken by one enemy on his far side.
The king is taken like any man, between two, except near his seat. On the seat he must be shut in on all four sides. On a square next to the seat he must be shut in on the three open sides.
The dark side wins the moment the king stands on any square at the edge of the board. The fair side wins the moment the king is taken.

When the king has one open road to the edge his player says so ('raichi', the Sami said to Linnaeus); with two open roads ('tuichu') the game is over, since only one can be shut. The board marks an open road, so nobody loses by not seeing it.
A side that cannot move loses. If the same position comes three times the game is drawn and the stakes go back. Either player may give the game up at any time.
The owner of the board chooses his side. A guest who is offered the king is being honoured.

The small board (Gaelic ports): 7 by 7 holes. The king on the middle hole with four men, one on each side of him; eight attackers, two in a line at the middle of each side. The same rules, but the king must reach a corner hole, only the king may stand on a corner, and an empty corner counts as an enemy like the empty seat.
games.card_run: Card 1: who he is, whose board it is, the side you are given, the stake. Then the board. Last card: the end, and what he says of it. Against a lord there is one more card before your winning move: take the game, or make a false move and let him have it.
games.stakes: 1 to 12 d among crews on a quay. 12 to 60 d in a hall, or a thing of that worth: a comb, a string of glass beads, a knife, a set of pieces. A lord does not play a merchant for silver; he plays for the evening, and a merchant who beats him should do it gently. Canute's game shows what a bad loser with an army can do.
games.what_it_gives: Silver from equals. Standing in a hall, where skill at the board is a thing a man is known for. A friend: a man you have played three times keeps a seat and his news for you. A riddle for the chest (the three tafl riddles are given by tafl players). From a lord you let win: his good will, which is worth more than the stake.
games.picture: A low bench in a hall by firelight: a squared wooden board with dark pieces crowded round a taller king in the middle and pale pieces at the four sides, one hand reaching in, a horn cup at the board's edge.
games.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tafl_games (Gokstad, Ballinderry, Birka, Lindisfarne, Linnaeus 1732 and the 1811 mistranslation, Alea evangelii, the sagas); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alea_evangelii; da.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hnefatafl (Trondheim); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birka_female_Viking_warrior; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salme_ships; Heimskringla, Saga of Olaf Haraldson ch. 162-163 (Laing 1844); the riddle from Vigfusson and Powell 1883 as in texts_793.json (t-gest-19). York, Toftanes, Hedeby, the Exeter maxims and Rigsthula are from memory, not checked (?). The 7 by 7 layout and corner rule are the modern reconstruction of the Irish brandubh.

games.name: Mill (nine men's morris)
games.screen: a board on screen: three squares one inside another, 24 points, 18 pieces
evidence: The other side of the Gokstad board (buried about 900 to 905 (?)) is cut for nine men's morris. The same man's board served both games.
The Toftanes board in the Faroes (900s) is said to be the same: tafl on one face, mill on the other (?).

The game is far older than the North's use of it: Ovid may mean a small form of it, about AD 8. Later it is scratched into the cloister seats of Canterbury, Gloucester, Norwich, Salisbury and Westminster.
The rules are first written in Alfonso of Castile's book of games, 1283, which also shows a form played with dice.
games.not_known: How the Northmen played on the Gokstad board is written nowhere. That Frisians, Franks and English of these years played it is likely and unproved. The rules here are the plain medieval ones. 'Flying' with the last three men is a habit some later players have and others do not; it is left out. That a move closing two mills takes only one man is the game's choice.
games.where: Anywhere a board can be scratched: a hatch cover, a quay stone, a bench end. A boatman's and a boy's game, played while waiting for wind or tide.
how_it_plays: The board is three squares one inside another, joined by a line through the middle of each side: 24 points where lines meet or end. Each player has nine men.
Setting: in turn each player sets one man on any empty point, until all eighteen are down. The guest sets first.

Three of your men in a row along one line is a mill. Each time you close a mill, by setting or by moving, you take one enemy man off the board for good. You may not take a man who stands in a mill unless all his men stand in mills.
Moving: when all the men are set, the players in turn move one man along a line to the next point, if it is empty. No man jumps.
A mill may be opened by moving a man out of it and closed again by moving him back on a later turn. Every closing takes a man.
A move that closes two mills at once still takes one man.
You lose when you have only two men left, or when it is your turn and none of your men can move.
If the same position comes three times, or twenty turns pass with no man taken, the game is drawn and the stakes go back.

setup.next_to: two points are next to each other when they follow one another in a mill

games.card_run: Card 1: who he is and what he plays for. Then the board. Last card: the end, and the talk that went with it.
games.stakes: A cup of ale, a penny, at most 6 d. Among a crew: who fetches the water, who takes the cold watch.
games.what_it_gives: Little silver. It is the cheap way to a friend among the harbour's small people (a ferryman, a porter, a boy who sees every ship come in), and they pay in harbour talk: who is in, who left in a hurry, what the toll man is like today. Played with one of your own men while waiting for wind, it lifts the crew's heart.
games.picture: A hatch cover with three squares scratched one inside another, white pebbles and black pebbles on the corners and line ends, a boy and an old ferryman squatting over it, the river behind.
games.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tafl_games (the Gokstad board's reverse); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nine_men%27s_morris (rules, Ovid, the cloister seats, Libro de los juegos 1283, flying as a variant); Toftanes from memory (?).

games.name: A riddle match
games.screen: cards only (the riddle's words, and the chest's palette to answer from)
evidence: The Exeter Book, copied about 970, holds some ninety riddles in English verse. Many end with a dare: 'Say what I am called.'

The Latin riddles of Aldhelm (died 709), Tatwine (died 734), Eusebius and Boniface were the monks' game of the century before the game begins. Thirty-odd of these and of Symphosius are in the library.

Alcuin wrote a riddling dialogue with Charlemagne's son Pippin in the 790s ('What is a letter? The keeper of history. What is a ship? A wandering house.'): the Frankish court played at this in the very years the game starts.

The match as a contest is in the old poems. In Vafthrudnismal Odin and a giant stake their heads on questions of lore. In Hervarar saga (written in the 1200s, the riddles perhaps older) Gestumblindi, who is Odin, riddles King Heidrek to save his neck. Both end the same way: Odin asks what he whispered in his dead son's ear, a question only the asker can answer, and the loser cries foul. These riddles are in the chest (r-gest, r-vafth, r-alv).
games.not_known: No account of an ordinary riddle match between ordinary people survives. The poems stake heads and are about gods; the Exeter riddles are a book, not the record of an evening. That people set riddles to each other over drink is read from the riddles' own dare and from the poems. Turn about, three each, is the game's form.
games.where: A hall on a feast evening; a minster's guest-house, where the riddles are Latin; an ale-house with a man who has the name of a setter; aboard at anchor with a talkative crewman.
how_it_plays: Two take turns to set, three riddles each. The host or the challenger sets first.
When he sets, the card gives the riddle's words. You answer by laying a thing from your palette on it. You have three tries at each riddle.

A right answer is a point to the one who answered. When your three tries are gone the point is his, and the riddle goes into your chest to rest, as chest riddles do: you may bring him the answer on a later visit.

When you set, you may only set a riddle you have solved yourself. You choose one from the chest. The card says, as a word, how likely he is to know it: a riddle of his own people and tongue he likely knows; a Latin one in a Norse hall, or a Norse one in a minster, he likely does not. A riddle he has heard from you before he always knows.
If he cannot answer, the point is yours.

A question only the asker can answer (what is in my hold, what did I whisper) is foul. The room shouts it down and the match is lost. It is offered as an option when you are losing, and it is how Odin wins.
Most points after three each wins. If they are level, each sets one more until one man misses and the other does not.
The match needs his tongue: yours at 0.5 or more, or a crewman who has it and may answer one riddle for you.
games.card_run: Card 1: the challenge and the stake. Cards 2 to 7: his riddle and your answer, then your riddle and his answer, three times. Card 8: the end, the stake paid, and the riddle he gives you to take away.
games.stakes: A cup for every miss, in a hall. A seat nearer the fire. A ring, a knife or a thing worth 12 to 40 d from a host who likes the game. In a minster nothing is staked: the brothers play for the pleasure of it. Heads are for gods.
games.what_it_gives: Standing: a riddle answered to the man who set it is the deed 'won_riddle', which the Norse and the Irish weigh most. The host's good will. Always a riddle: win or lose, you carry away the one that beat you or one he thinks will. A gift on a clear win. In a minster, leave to read or copy a text.
games.picture: A long hall at night, one man standing with a horn in his hand and his other hand raised, the benches leaning in to listen, a merchant in a short Frisian cloak frowning into the fire.
games.source: Exeter Book riddles (Tupper 1910) and the Latin riddles as in texts_793.json; Hervarar saga, Vafthrudnismal, Alvissmal as in riddles_793.json (Vigfusson and Powell 1883; Bellows 1923); Alcuin, Disputatio Pippini cum Albino (the two answers are my own plain rendering of the Latin, from memory (?)); 'Say what I am called' is my own rendering of the Old English close; Design/npc_text_encounters.md 2.9 and card 24 for the setter.

games.name: The harp goes round
games.screen: cards only (the song's first lines on the card)
evidence: Whitby, about 680: at a feast, when it was agreed that each should sing in turn, the cowherd Caedmon would get up when he saw the harp coming toward him and go home (Bede, 731, book 4 chapter 24).

Frisia, the 780s: Bernlef, a blind man, was loved by his neighbours because he could sing well the deeds of the men of old and the wars of kings. Liudger healed him and he sang psalms after (Altfrid's Life of Liudger, about 840).

Alcuin to an English bishop, 797: let the reader be heard at the priests' table, not the harper; the Fathers, not the songs of the heathen. 'What has Ingeld to do with Christ?' So the brothers were listening to lays of old kings at dinner.
Einhard, about 830: Charlemagne had the old songs of the deeds and wars of the ancient kings written down (chapter 29). The book is lost.

The harp itself is a six-stringed lyre held on the knee: Trossingen (about 560 to 580), Sutton Hoo (about 610 to 635), Cologne (about 700), and parts of others are listed from Dorestad, Elisenhof, Hedeby, Birka, York and Ribe (listed only: not checked piece by piece (?)).
Beowulf's hall has a singer who makes a new song on the day's deed. Harald of Norway (died 1066) counted the harp and verse among his eight skills (?).
games.not_known: No tune survives. How a lay was sung to six strings is guessed from pictures and from later custom. The game writes no music for it (its sound is public-domain recordings only): the song is its words on the card. How a room judged a song is not recorded; the three fits below are the game's.
games.where: A hall, an ale-house, a guest-house on a feast evening. Among Frisians, English, Saxons and Northmen alike; in a minster's guest-house the songs are God's, or should be.
how_it_plays: The harp comes down the bench and each takes it in turn. When it comes to you there are three things to do.

Sing: choose a poem or song from your chest, in a tongue the room knows (yours at 0.5 or more). Or let a crewman sing, if you have one who can. Or pass the harp on, or slip out as Caedmon did: it costs nothing but a little pride.

The room weighs the song by three fits. New: it has not been sung in this port before. Theirs: it is their own people's matter (old kings in a Frisian, Saxon or Norse hall; God's making in a guest-house). The day's: it suits the day (a lament at a funeral ale, a riddle-song at a wedding, the sea at a sailors' bench).
Three fits: the host gives a gift and asks you back. Two: a full cup and good will. One: they are polite. None: they hear you out.
A song for a song: after yours, someone answers with one of theirs. If you or a crewman can hold it (letters, runes or a good ear), it goes into the chest: one new text an evening at most.
A heathen lay sung to monks pleases the brothers and not the abbot: his feeling falls as theirs rises.
The same song in the same port within a year counts as no fit at all.
games.card_run: Card 1: the room, the day, who sang before you and what. Card 2: your choice of song (three from the chest that could fit, the fit of each as a word), a crewman, or pass. Card 3: how it was taken, the gift, and the song given back.
games.stakes: No silver. An evening, and your name in that room.
games.what_it_gives: Standing in that hall. A gift from the host on a good night (a ring, a length of cloth, 20 to 40 d worth). A new text for the chest, which is the real prize: songs are news that does not go stale. The host as a friend. When a crewman sings and is praised, the crew's heart.
games.picture: A bench in a smoky hall, a small six-stringed lyre passing from one pair of hands to the next, the next man half risen as if to leave, the host watching from the high seat.
games.source: Bede, Historia ecclesiastica IV.24; Altfrid, Vita Liudgeri (Bernlef); Alcuin, letter of 797 (Duemmler no. 124) (?); Einhard, Vita Karoli 29; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Saxon_lyre (the finds and their dates, the six strings); Beowulf as in texts_793.json. Bede, Altfrid, Alcuin and Einhard are given in my own plain words from memory of the Latin, not quoted from any translation.

games.name: The cups (sumbel)
games.takes: an evening, and the next morning if you drain all three
evidence: The word is in three tongues: Old English 'symbel' (Beowulf), Old Saxon 'sumbal' (the Heliand, about 830), Old Norse 'sumbl' (Lokasenna). It means a drinking feast.
In Beowulf the lady of the hall carries the cup to the king and then to each man by rank, and Beowulf makes his boast over it before the fight.

Snorri on the feasts of Trondelag about 950 (written about 1230): 'first Odin's goblet was emptied for victory and power to his king; thereafter, Niord's and Freyja's goblets for peace and a good season. Then it was the custom of many to empty the brage-goblet; and then the guests emptied a goblet to the memory of departed friends, called the remembrance goblet.' (Laing's note: the brage-goblet is the one 'over which vows were made'.)

At such a feast the Christian king Hakon made the sign of the cross over Odin's cup. Earl Sigurd told the angry farmers: 'He is blessing the full goblet in the name of Thor, by making the sign of his hammer over it before he drinks it.'

At Svein Forkbeard's funeral ale, about 986 (?), the cups were to his father, then 'Christ's health', then Saint Michael; and over them the Jomsborg chiefs vowed to drive Earl Hakon from Norway. But 'the next morning, when the Jomsborg vikings had slept off their drink, they thought they had spoken more than enough.'
Havamal on ale is in the library: 'Worse food for the journey he brings not afield than an over-drinking of ale' (havamal_011; also havamal_012).
games.not_known: Snorri wrote three hundred years after Hakon and may have tidied a heathen feast into a rite. The order of the cups, and whether ordinary men vowed over them as chiefs did, is his word and the poems'. Scholars (Bauschatz 1976, Pollington 2003) built 'the sumbel' as a rite from these; it may have been looser. What Frisians and Franks said over a cup in 793 is not recorded.
games.where: A lord's or a chief's hall on a feast evening, a funeral ale, a wedding ale. In Christian halls the cups are Christ's and the saints'. In an ale-house the same thing happens without the high seat: three cups and a loose tongue.
how_it_plays: Three cups go round, and each is a card. First the card says where you have been seated: by the door, on the middle bench, near the high seat. That is your standing here, shown plainly.

The first cup is the blessing. In a heathen hall it is drunk to Odin for victory and the king's power, or to Njord and Frey for peace and a good year. In a Christian hall it is Christ's health and Saint Michael's. A Christian in a heathen hall may drink as they do (the hall warms; his Christian crew mutter), sign the cup with the cross (the hall chills, unless a friend there says it is the hammer: likely if the host is your friend, doubtful if not), or pass it on untasted with a good word (pride only).

The second cup is the vow cup. You may make a vow before the hall: the card offers two or three, taken from what is truly open to you (a load to bring by a named feast, your debt cleared by Michaelmas, a crossing before the first frost). A vow is written down with its day. Or you may praise the host, which is safe and small. Or drink and say nothing.
A vow too big for your boat may be questioned by the hall's challenger, the man who sits at the lord's feet. Then you answer with a deed you have really done, or take the vow back and lose face.

The third cup is the memory cup. You name a dead man: a crewman you lost, your father, or one of the host's dead if you know who they were. A lost shipmate named before his fellows lifts the crew's heart. The host's own dead, rightly named, lifts his.

At each cup you choose to drain it or to sip. Draining honours the cup. After two drained cups your bench-mate's tongue is loose and you hear one true thing. After three, yours is loose too: you let slip one price you know, and you lose the next morning.
A vow kept by its day is told in that hall and carried by the ships. A vow broken is carried faster.
games.card_run: Card 1: the seat, the first cup and its three ways. Card 2: the vow cup and the vows on offer. Card 3: the memory cup and the names you could say. A fourth card only if the challenger speaks, or the morning after three drained cups.
games.stakes: No silver is laid. You stake your word. A vow kept is worth more than a cargo here; a vow broken follows you from port to port.
games.what_it_gives: Standing: a kept vow is the surest way to rise in a hall, and it rises in every hall that hears. A true rumour from the bench. The host's friendship and a seat higher next time. The crew's heart, from the memory cup. It costs a morning if you drain all three, and one of your price secrets.
games.picture: A woman in a good dress carrying a horn in both hands down the length of a hall toward the high seat, men on the benches watching it come, firelight, one man with his hand half raised over the horn.
games.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symbel (the word, Beowulf 489-675, Heliand 3339, Lokasenna 8, Bauschatz, Pollington); Heimskringla, Hakon the Good's Saga ch. 16 and 18, and King Olaf Trygvason's Saga ch. 39 (Laing 1844: gutenberg.org/ebooks/598; Snorri's Norse has the god Frey where Laing wrote Freyja (?)); Havamal 11 (Bellows 1923) as in texts_793.json.

games.name: Matching men (flyting)
games.comes_as: a card at drink (act:drink, act:feast) or when a man in hall takes against you
evidence: Beowulf, fitts IX and X (in the library: beowulf_09, beowulf_10): Unferth, who sits at the king's feet, taunts the guest with a swimming match he lost. Beowulf answers: 'My good friend Unferth, sure freely and wildly, / Thou fuddled with beer of Breca hast spoken', tells it his own way, and adds that Unferth killed his own brothers.

Norway, about 1120 (?) (written about 1230): the ale is bad and the room is dull, so King Eystein says: 'It is a common custom over the ale-table to compare one person with another, and now let us do so.' He and his brother Sigurd match wrestling, swimming, skates, the bow, looks and law, then a journey to the Jordan against harbours and a hall built at home. 'Thereupon both were silent, and there was anger on both sides.'
The Edda's Lokasenna and Harbardsljod are the same game played by gods: each stanza an insult, each answer a worse one. The charges are cowardice, unmanliness and shameful kin.

Roskilde 1026 (?): 'Runnest thou away, Ulf the coward?' 'Thou didst not call me Ulf the coward, when I hastened to thy help while the Swedes were beating thee like a dog.' The earl was dead by morning.
The laws of Norway and Iceland, written down in the 1100s and 1200s, set full outlawry on a few named words (?). There was a line, and men knew where it was.
games.not_known: How a winner was chosen is not recorded: the room's laughter and the loser's silence is the usual reading, and that the winner drank and then offered the loser the cup is a modern summary (?). The poems are art, not minutes. Three rounds is the game's form. Nothing of the kind is recorded for Franks or Frisians.
games.where: A Norse or English hall at drink, an ale-house full of crews, a feast. It needs a room to judge it.
how_it_plays: It begins when a man compares himself with you over the ale, or you with him. Both must take it up: it is a game only while both are laughing.
Three rounds. In each he says his line, and you choose one answer.

A true boast: one of your own deeds. The card offers up to three from your own record (a crossing made, a storm outlived, the debt paid, a riddle won, a raider outrun, a lord's commission kept). The rarer the deed in this room, the better it lands.

A turn: you answer his boast with what you know of him (his wreck, his lost case, the port he cannot go back to). It is offered only if you truly know something, and it is strongest when it is news to the room.

A swollen boast: a deed you have not done. It lands hard if believed. If anyone who knows better calls it, you lose this round and the next. Far from home it will likely pass; among men who know you it is doubtful.
Or let it go with a laugh: you lose the round and keep his good will.

Every turn comes mild or hard. The hard word (coward, no man, shameful kin) surely wins the round, but he may stop laughing. Then the game is over and he wants amends in silver, or your name is spoken at the next thing.
The room gives each round to one man. Two rounds of three win. The winner drinks, then hands the cup to the loser; a winner who does it well gains more than the win.
games.card_run: Card 1: who he is, what he says, whether you take it up. Cards 2 to 4: his line, your answers with how each is likely to land. Card 5: the cup handed over, or the bench pushed back.
games.stakes: Your name in that room. Sometimes men lay wagers on the two of you and the winner is given a share: 6 to 20 d.
games.what_it_gives: Standing in the hall, and the deed you boasted of travels: it is told as news where the ships from here go. Often a friend, in the man you matched and did not shame. A share of the wagers. Or a feud, if you used the hard word.
games.picture: Two men on their feet either side of a hall fire, one pointing with a horn, the other with thumbs in his belt and his chin up, the benches laughing, one old man at the lord's feet not laughing.
games.source: Beowulf fitts IX-X (J. Lesslie Hall 1892) as in texts_793.json; Heimskringla, Saga of Sigurd the Crusader ch. 25, and Saga of Olaf Haraldson ch. 163 (Laing 1844: gutenberg.org/ebooks/598); Lokasenna and Harbardsljod (Bellows 1923), named, not quoted; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flyting (the charges; the winner's cup (?)). The laws on words are from memory (?).

games.name: Wrestling, on the green or in the water
games.comes_as: a card at a fair, a thing, a beach market or a feast day; the ducking match in any harbour on a warm day
evidence: King Sigurd to his brother, Norway about 1120 (?): 'Do you remember that I was always able to throw you when we wrestled, although you are a year older?' and 'Do you remember that I could drag you under water, when we swam together, as often as I pleased?'

Nidaros, autumn 999 (?): the Icelander Kjartan swims out against the best man in the river, 'seizes hold of his foot, and dives with him under water'. They go under three times, each longer, until Kjartan is nearly drowned. The man is King Olaf, who gives him a cloak. (Laing took the passage from another manuscript of the kings' sagas; it is also in Laxdaela saga.)

A Norwegian harbour, about 1130 (?): an Icelander 'amused himself by drawing those under water who could not swim so well as himself; and at that the spectators laughed', until the king did it to him.
Beowulf and Breca, as boys, swam the sea for a boast (beowulf_09, beowulf_10 in the library).

Charlemagne loved swimming and nobody could beat him at it; at Aachen he bathed with his sons, his nobles and his guard, sometimes a hundred men in the water together (Einhard, about 830, chapter 22). This is the one witness from the game's own years and its own shore.

In Snorri's Edda (about 1220) Thor wrestles an old woman who is Old Age, and going down on one knee is a fall (?). The sagas have wrestling at assemblies; the three later Icelandic styles are the back-hold, the loose grip and the trouser grip.
games.not_known: The holds, and what counted as a fall, are known only from later Iceland; the modern rule (a fall is touching the ground between elbow and knee) is modern. For Frisians, Franks and English nothing is known beyond that men wrestled and swam. The three choices below are the game's way of making a bout readable.
games.where: A fair, a thing-place, a beach market, a feast-day green; the ducking match off any quay or beach in warm weather.
how_it_plays: A man offers a bout. You may take it yourself or put up one of your crew; then it is his strength that counts and his name that is made.
It is the best of three falls. A fall is a knee or more on the ground.
For each fall both men choose one of three, unseen: Grip (close and lift), Hook (take his leg), Wait (keep your feet and turn his move).
Grip beats Wait. Wait beats Hook. Hook beats Grip. If both choose the same, the stronger man has the fall; the card says who that likely is.

Before each fall the card gives one true thing about him: 'a head taller, and slow' (he will likely Grip), 'light, and watching your feet' (Hook), 'an old hand who lets you come' (Wait). After each fall it tells what he did.

In the water it is the same three falls with other names: Seize (pull him under), Dive (slip his hold and take him from below), Tread (save your breath). Seize beats Tread, Tread beats Dive, Dive beats Seize. A fall is the first man to break for air.
You may give a bout up at any time. In the water, giving up is coming up.
After the last fall the loser takes the winner's hand, or does not. The card offers a good word or a grudge.
games.card_run: Card 1: the man, the wagers round the ring, yourself or a crewman. Cards 2 to 4: what you see of him, your choice, the fall. Card 5: the hand, the wagers paid.
games.stakes: Onlookers' wagers: 2 to 24 d, of which the winner has half. At a fair a thing is put up: a knife, an axe, a cloak. In the water, a small hurt if you stay down too long.
games.what_it_gives: Silver from the wagers. A name on that shore: men who saw it remember you, and the Norse weigh it most. The crew's heart when your man wins. A friend in the man you threw cleanly.
games.picture: A ring of people on trampled grass by a beached boat, two men stripped to the waist locked chest to chest, one lifting; or two heads and a splash in harbour water with men cheering from a ship's side.
games.source: Heimskringla: Saga of Sigurd the Crusader ch. 25 and 36, King Olaf Trygvason's Saga ch. 88 (Laing 1844: gutenberg.org/ebooks/598; ch. 88's swimming is marked by Laing as taken from Codex Frisianus); Einhard, Vita Karoli 22 (my own plain words, not quoted); Beowulf as in texts_793.json; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glima (the three styles, the modern fall); Snorri's Edda (Thor and Elli) from memory (?).

games.name: The horse fight
games.comes_as: a card at a Norse thing-place or gathering in late summer
evidence: The Haggeby stone, Uppland (U 664), possibly of the 500s: a ship with rowers on one face, two horses fighting on the other. It lay face down in the church floor until 1863 and is now in the Historical Museum in Stockholm.

Njal's saga (written about 1280, of Iceland about 975 (?)): 'Now men ride to the horse-fight, and a very great crowd is gathered together there.' Each owner drives his own horse, with 'a great riding-rod in his hand'. 'Then the horses run at one another, and bit each other long, so that there was no need for any one to touch them, and that was the greatest sport.' Then two men shove their horse at Gunnar, he throws them down, one of them strikes out his horse's eye, he strikes back with the rod, and a feud has begun.
Other sagas tell the same kind of day: Grettir's, Killer-Glum's, and the tale of Thorstein Staff-struck, who has his name from a blow at a horse fight (?).
In Norway such meets ('skeid') were kept in the upland valleys into the 1800s (?).
games.not_known: Every written account is Icelandic and three hundred years younger than the fight it tells of. That Danes, Svear and Norwegians of the 800s held such fights rests on one carved stone and on late custom. No rule for judging is recorded: a horse that turns and runs has lost, as far as the sagas show. Nothing of the kind is known among Franks, Frisians or English.
games.where: Norse places with a thing-place or open ground, late in summer, between the hay and the corn (?). Not in towns of other peoples.
how_it_plays: You are a watcher with silver, not an owner. Two stallions are led up, each with his owner behind him holding a rod.

Look them over. Of each horse you are told one thing freely (his age, his scars, how he stands). A second thing costs a question to a man beside you. A third you have only if you know the owner already.
Lay a wager with a named man on one horse, or lay none and watch.
There are three clashes, a card each. After the first and the second you may hold, add to your wager if a man will take it, or buy yourself out for half of it.
A horse that turns away twice, or will not close, has lost. If both are still fighting after three clashes the owners part them and the wagers go back.

One fight in four, a rod comes down on the other man's horse, or on the other man. Then you may step between them (a blow is likely; both owners remember who stopped it), stand ready to bear witness at the thing (one friend, one enemy), or go, with your wager handed back.
games.card_run: Card 1: the two horses and their owners, what you can see. Card 2: the wager. Cards 3 to 5: the clashes. A sixth card when the rods come down.
games.stakes: 4 to 40 d with a named man. Farmers wager in cloth, butter, a sheep.
games.what_it_gives: Silver. A horse-meet gathers a whole district, so one talk there is worth three: the price of horses and hides, who is at law with whom, who is fitting out a ship. A friend and an enemy if you bear witness. Standing with everyone if you part two men before iron is drawn.
games.picture: Two stallions reared against each other in a ring of people on a late-summer field, each with a man behind him holding a long rod, a third man in a red tunic shouldering in.
games.source: sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upplands_runinskrifter_664 (the Haggeby stone); Njal's saga ch. 58 'How Gunnar's horse fought' (Dasent 1861: sagadb.org/brennu-njals_saga.en; ch. 59 in other editions); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horse_fighting (hestavig among the Icelanders). The other sagas, the season and the Norwegian skeid are from memory (?).

games.name: A day with the hawks
games.comes_as: a card after act:gift, act:audience or a commission kept for a lord, a reeve or a king's man
evidence: The Frankish church council of 742 forbade clergy to hunt with hounds or to keep hawks and falcons (?). They were keeping them.

About 745 Boniface sent King Aethelbald of Mercia a hawk and two falcons with his letter. A few years later King Aethelberht of Kent wrote to ask Boniface for two falcons bold enough to take cranes, since few such birds were to be had in Kent (?).
Asser, 893: King Alfred himself taught his falconers, hawkers and dog-keepers (chapter 76) (?).
Maldon, 991: before the fight a young man let his hawk fly from his hand to the wood, and by that it was known he would not flinch.
The Bayeux Tapestry, 1070s: Harold rides with a hawk on his fist.
An Icelander's speech about 1024 (?) names the fitting gifts for a king: 'hawks or horses, tents or sails'. Falcons are a good in the game's table, carried from the north to the lords of the south.
games.not_known: No account of a day's hawking survives from these years. Which birds were flown at what is pieced together from the letters (falcons at cranes), from bones and from later books. Hoods came later, from the east (?): the birds here ride bare-headed. The three flights are the game's way of telling a day.
games.where: The household of an English or Frankish lord, reeve or king's man; a Norse chief's. Out of the town, on the marsh or the river meadows. By invitation only, and never a bishop's (he has no hawks, the council says).
how_it_plays: The lord asks you to ride out with him. It takes the day. You carry no bird: what you choose each time is where to put yourself.
There are three flights, a card each: a hawk from the fist at duck or hare in the morning; a falcon at heron or crane at midday; a bird that will not come back in the afternoon.

At each flight choose one. Ride at the lord's side and speak of what you came for: your best chance to be heard, but a word at the wrong moment spoils the flight (the card says how the moment looks, as a word). Hold back with the falconer and the dogs: you learn birds, and he remembers you. Mark the fall: ride hard to where the quarry comes down; a tumble is possible, and the lord thanks the man who finds his bird.

Each flight earns 0, 1 or 2 of his favour. With 4 or more at the day's end he grants one thing: he hears your matter, gives a letter, speaks a word at the toll, or sets you a commission. With 2 or 3 you are asked again. With less, nothing is lost but the day.
Having held back with the falconer once, you can tell a good bird from a poor one when you buy in the north.
He will always ask whether you can bring him birds.
games.card_run: Card 1: the asking, and what you mean to get from him. Cards 2 to 4: the three flights. Card 5: what he grants, and the birds he wants.
games.stakes: A day, and a gift beforehand. No silver is wagered. The risk is a word at the wrong moment.
games.what_it_gives: A friend in a hall where a merchant is not often heard. A commission for falcons at a premium. Court news, a season fresher than the quay's. A word at the toll or a letter, on a good day. The falconer's eye for a bird.
games.picture: Riders on a river meadow in morning mist, a lord with a hawk on his gloved fist, a falconer on foot with two hounds, a merchant on a borrowed horse a length behind, cranes rising far off.
games.source: Concilium Germanicum 742, c. 2 (?); Boniface's letters (Tangl nos. 69 and 105 (?)); Asser, Life of Alfred 76 (?); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Falconry (Maldon 991, the Bayeux Tapestry); Heimskringla, Saga of Olaf Haraldson (Laing 1844: the speech against giving the king Grimsey). The council, the letters and Asser are from memory, in my own words, not checked.

at_home: What a Frisian of Dorestad would know in 793, as far as the evidence goes: dice and knucklebones on the quay; the harp in the hall and songs of old kings (Bernlef); riddles among the clerks at Utrecht (?); the cups, with Christ's name over them; wrestling and swimming, as everywhere. Tafl he learns from Danes and Northmen. No board has been reported from Dorestad that I know of (?).

left_out.why: The Roman race game with dice on a board, the ancestor of backgammon, is the Franks' and the churchmen's board game, and 'taefl' in English can mean it. No rules or board of 793 to 1066 could be checked; the fine Gloucester set is about 1100 (?). It should be the Frankish answer to tafl once someone has the sources.
It reaches the North at the very end of these years (?). Snorri's 'chess' for Canute in 1026 is a word of his own time (about 1230).
Known only from Icelandic sagas, with no rules.
Bone skates are common finds in the towns of these years (?), but it is a way to cross ice and a child's joy, not a contest with a stake. It belongs to the winter cards.

left_out.what: Staking one's own freedom at dice
left_out.why: Tacitus tells it of an older time. The player can never do it; another man may, once in a long while, and then it is a season at the oars.

needs: No act id exists for the contests (matching men, wrestling, the horse fight, hawking). They are written to come as cards from drink, feast, gift, audience and at a thing-place or fair. If an act is wanted, it would be 'contest'.

Deeds that would help and do not exist in reputation_793.json: won_game (a win at the board or in the ring, seen by a room), kept_vow and broke_vow (the vow cup), sang_well (the harp). Until then a vow is wired as a commission (kept_commission, broke_commission exist) and a riddle win as won_riddle.
Condition variables that would help: the count of the player's own deeds for the true boasts (crossings made, storms outlived), and whether a text has been sung in a port before.
The flags named in 'in_verbs' (vow_<name>, flyting_feud_<port>, knows_falcons) are suggestions, not yet read by anything.
Two small boards to draw and code: the 9 by 9 tafl board (and its 7 by 7 form) and the mill board. Everything else is cards.
